You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

  "text": "From: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 10:15:00 -0500

Question for the group: How do I figure out if I'm using my shelf space
efficiently? I need something that shows me, for each genre and format:
- What percentage of total circulations it has
- What percentage of the collection it is
- What percentage of total shelf space it occupies

Does anyone else need this?

Maria
P.S. Does anyone know if the new Marvel movie is any good?
===
From: thomas.wright@augusta-reed.lib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 11:02:33 -0500

YES, I need this too. As a cataloger, I'm always trying to convince our
director to reallocate space from low-circulation genres to high-circulation
ones. Having actual data would be game-changing.

Currently I pull reports manually and make spreadsheets. It's tedious.

My kid is obsessed with dinosaur books right now. I'm reading "The Rise and
Fall of the Dinosaurs" at bedtime. Apparently T-Rex could bite through a
car. Fascinating bedtime reading.
===
From: susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, thomas.wright@augusta-reed.lib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 11:45:07 -0500

This is the "shelf space report" we've been talking about. The idea is:
for each genre and format of material, compare:
1. Percentage of total circulations
2. Percentage of the collection
3. Percentage of total shelf space

The report should be able to run per library and per system. This way branch
managers can see their local situation AND see how they compare to the system
average.

I just got back from the farmer's market. Got some amazing heirloom tomatoes.
Anyone tried making a tomato sandwich with just basil, salt, and bread?
Heaven on earth.
===
From: latoya.davidson@twinlakeslib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, thomas.wright@augusta-reed.lib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 12:30:55 -0500

I would need this at the system level for sure. When I look at Twin Lakes
as a whole, we might have too many romance novels in some branches and not
enough in others. Being able to redistribute based on data would help.

Can we also filter by date range? Like, what was the shelf space utilization
in Q1 vs. Q2? Seasons matter for our collection.

Also, my cat Mittens keeps knocking plants off my windowsill. I've moved the
plants but he finds new ones to knock over. Cats are ridiculous.
===
From: robert.chen@gapubliclib.org
To: latoya.davidson@twinlakeslib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 14:10:22 -0500

From a data perspective, we need to:
1. Count items per genre/format (this is the "percentage of collection")
2. Sum checkouts per genre/format (this is the "percentage of circulations")
3. Estimate shelf space per genre/format (this is the "percentage of shelf space")

The tricky part is #3. Shelf space isn't directly tracked in the database.
We'd need to estimate based on item dimensions or use item count as a proxy.

We can also add the per-library and per-system breakdown. That's just
adding GROUP BY clauses to the right levels.

Going to try that pesto recipe I found. Using the basil from my garden.
===
From: jennifer.durham@statesboro.lib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, thomas.wright@augusta-reed.lib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, latoya.davidson@twinlakeslib.org, robert.chen@gapubliclib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Shelf space vs. usage - help needed
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2009 15:20:00 -0500

I want this broken down per library AND per system. Our directors review
this data quarterly and need both views.

Also, can we include a "comparison" view that shows each library's breakdown
side by side? That would make it easy to spot outliers.

My sister is visiting from Atlanta this weekend. She's been begging me to
take her to Callaway Gardens. I haven't been since I was a kid.
===

  "text": "From: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 10:00:00 -0500

Quick question: Is there a way to track when records are deleted? We need
to be able to count and track record deletions (item records, patron
records) per location and per system. This is for auditing purposes.

Right now when something gets deleted, it just... disappears. No record.

Maria
===
From: george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 10:45:33 -0500

Yes, we absolutely need this. Last month our director asked for a report
of all patron records deleted in Q1 and I had to piece it together from
memory and email logs. Not professional.

We need:
- What type of record was deleted (item/patron/bib)
- When it was deleted
- Who deleted it
- Where they were located (which branch)
- Possibly why (status before deletion?)

My neighbor just got a new puppy. It's a golden doodle named Biscuit.
Apparently Biscuit has a taste for garden hose.

-George
===
From: robert.chen@gapubliclib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 11:30:00 -0500

This is actually a good idea from an auditing standpoint. Currently,
Evergreen does not log deletions - once something is deleted, it's gone.

To implement this, we'd need:
1. A trigger in the database that logs deletions to an audit table
2. Fields: record_type, record_id, deleted_by, deleted_at, location
3. A report interface to query this audit table

The report should show deletions per location and per system. We can
aggregate by date range, by user, by record type.

My laptop battery is at 2%. I need to plug in before I lose this draft.
===
From: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, robert.chen@gapubliclib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 12:15:00 -0500

I agree with George - this is about accountability. If we accidentally
delete something we shouldn't have, we need to be able to trace it.

Also, the deletion log would help with troubleshooting. "Why did this
patron's record disappear?" - check the log.

Taking my daughter to ballet class. She has a recital next week and
is very nervous.

-Dana
===
From: susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, robert.chen@gapubliclib.org, dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 13:40:00 -0500

From an administrative perspective, we need reports showing:
- Total deletions per period (month, quarter, year)
- Deletions by type (item vs patron vs other)
- Deletions by location
- Top users who delete the most records

This helps us identify if certain branches are deleting more than others,
which might indicate a process issue.

I'm reading "Where the Crawdads Sing" right now. The marsh descriptions
are beautiful.

-Susan
===
From: latoya.davidson@twinlakeslib.org
To: maria.rodriguez@dalton-whitman.lib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, robert.chen@gapubliclib.org, dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Tracking deletions - who deleted what?
Date: Fri, 24 Apr 2009 14:25:00 -0500

This also helps with compliance. Some libraries need to prove they're
handling data according to retention schedules. Being able to show
"we deleted 500 patron records on X date" is important for audits.

Can we also track attempted deletions that were denied? That would tell
us if someone is trying to delete things they shouldn't.

Trying out a new recipe for chicken tikka masala tonight. Fingers crossed.
===

Date: Mon, 27 Apr 2009 09:00:00 -0500

The system should count and track record deletions (e.g., item records,

Robert will implement the database triggers. Katherine will draft the

messages.content:
You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

 "document": {

  "text": "From: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Staff login difficulties - need for streamlined access
Date: Thu, 09 Apr 2009 09:15:32 -0500

Katherine,

Following up on yesterday's call, I wanted to share what we're seeing at the
front lines regarding staff login. At Ohoopee Regional, we have 15 public
service computers that are used by 8 different staff members throughout the
day. Currently, staff must type in their full username and password each time
they sit down. This creates two problems:

1. It slows down service - especially during busy periods, staff are spending
   precious seconds logging in instead of helping patrons.
2. It leads to security issues - staff get in a hurry and sometimes share
   passwords or leave terminals logged in.

We've seen other library systems implement card-swipe login for their ILS
terminals. The staff member simply swipes their employee ID badge and is logged
in immediately. This is much faster and more secure.

However, we also need to support the traditional username/password method - not
all staff may have ID cards, and we need a fallback. The system should support
BOTH methods - streamlined login (e.g. card swipe) AND traditional login
(individual login and password). The streamlined method should be optional but
available.

Can we add this to the requirements list?

Thanks,
Dana Peeler
Systems Librarian, Ohoopee Regional Library
===
From: susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org
To: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Staff login difficulties - need for streamlined access
Date: Thu, 09 Apr 2009 10:42:15 -0500

Dana,

I second this request. At Sara Hightower, we've had similar issues. One thing
to consider: even with card swipe, we need individual authentication. The
system must track WHICH staff member is logged in for audit purposes. The card
is just a convenient way to identify the person, but it shouldn't bypass
individual authentication entirely.

Also - and this is important - the system should not REQUIRE the streamlined
login. Some of our smaller branches may not have the infrastructure for card
readers. So the requirement should be: "The system supports (but does not
require) streamlined staff login methods."

We've also discussed role-based access through security groups. This relates to
the login requirement - when a staff member logs in (by any method), their
permissions should be determined by their assigned security group/role.
Administrators should be able to create and manage these groups.

- Susan
===
From: george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org
To: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Staff login difficulties - need for streamlined access
Date: Thu, 09 Apr 2009 11:20:08 -0500

Adding to this - we need user rights and privileges to be controlled through
security groups and/or "roles." This would allow access control for individuals,
workgroups, and arbitrary staff groups.

At Piedmont, we have several different types of staff:
- Front desk staff (can run basic reports, limited filters)
- Department heads (can create and modify templates)
- System administrators (full access to all reports and permissions)

Each of these should be a role that can be assigned to staff members. The system
should make it easy to administer these roles - changing someone's permissions
should be a simple matter of changing their role assignment, not modifying
individual permissions.

George Tuttle
Assistant Director, Piedmont Regional Library
===
From: katherine.gregory@gapubliclib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: SUMMARY: Staff login thread - adding to requirements doc
Date: Fri, 10 Apr 11:03:45 -0500

Thanks everyone for the input. I'm summarizing the key requirements from this
thread and will add them to our growing list:

1. System supports (but does not require) streamlined staff login methods,
   e.g. card swipe or individual login/password.
2. User rights and privileges controlled through security groups/roles.
3. Access control for individuals, workgroups, and arbitrary staff groups.
4. Easy administration of roles and permissions.

I'll make sure these are tracked in our requirements matrix.

- Katherine"
 }
}

  "text": "From: la.toyadavidson@twinlakeslib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Cc: finance.committee@gapl.org
Subject: Financial reporting requirements - discussion thread
Date: Mon, 13 Jul 2009 09:15:00 -0500

Hi everyone,

I've been working with our finance department at Twin Lakes to understand their
reporting needs. They've identified several requirements that we should
incorporate into our specifications. I'm sharing them here for discussion.

Key needs:
1. Value of items report - staff should be able to get the value of items
   based on data in item records. This could be the entire collection, or a
   portion. For example, they want to be able to get:
   - Value of all items with status "longoverdue"
   - Value of all DVDs in children's collection
   - Value of entire collection

2. Financial reports - staff need reports on:
   - Patron account balances by patron, home library, and system
   - Fines and charges accrued per time period (last 12 months, YTD, last month)
   - Fines waived per time period and per branch
   - Payments made per time period and per payment method (staff desk,
     self-check, OPAC)

3. Audit trail - system must maintain a ledger of patron payments, including
   which charges payments are applied to, to facilitate reconciliation.

4. Compliance - all reports and data archiving must comply with standard
   accounting practice and state, county, and municipal auditing requirements.

Thoughts?

LaToya
===
From: george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org
To: la.toyadavidson@twinlakeslib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Cc: finance.committee@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Financial reporting requirements - discussion thread
Date: Mon, 13 Jul 2009 10:30:22 -0500

LaToya,

These are spot on. I want to add a few things from our perspective:

- The financial audit trail is CRITICAL for our finance department. They need
  to be able to trace every payment back to the specific charge it was applied
  to. Without this, we can't reconcile our accounts properly.

- Regarding the "value of items report" - the data is already in the item
  records (purchase price field). We just need the system to be able to query
  and aggregate this. This should be straightforward.

- On compliance - we need to ensure that data archiving follows state and local
  requirements. Some data needs to be retained for 7 years for audit purposes.
  The system needs to enforce retention policies.

George
===
From: susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org
To: la.toyadavidson@twinlakeslib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Cc: finance.committee@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Financial reporting requirements - discussion thread
Date: Mon, 13 Jul 2009 11:45:01 -0500

I agree with everything. A few additional points:

- The financial data is attached to patron records AND item records. So when
  we query for financial reports, we need to be able to join these data sources.

- For fines and charges, the staff should be able to query patron accounts
  with balances greater than X dollars. This is useful for identifying accounts
  that need attention.

- The financial reports need to show payments by method - cash, credit card,
  check, etc. This helps with daily reconciliation.

- Fines waived should be tracked per library because each library has its own
  budget for waived fines.

Susan
===
From: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org
To: la.toyadavidson@twinlakeslib.org, george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: Re: Financial reporting requirements - discussion thread
Date: Mon, 13 Jul 2009 14:20:33 -0500

Adding from the staff perspective:

- We need to easily query patron accounts with balances greater than X dollars.
  Right now it takes forever to find these accounts manually.

- Financial information needs to be easily updatable. When a patron makes a
  payment at the front desk, we need the system to reflect that immediately.

- Payments tracking by library is important for our end-of-month reports. Each
  branch needs to be able to see what payments were collected at their location.

Dana
===

   record) in the entire collection or a portion. Examples: value of all items

   - Fines waived per time period and per branch
   - Payments made per time period and per payment method (staff desk,

5. AUDIT TRAIL:

- Katherine"

1. QUERY TOOL: We need a user-friendly interface for designing queries against
   all record types. Staff should be able to select fields to query, select
   values from picklists, use regular expressions from a dropdown, and use
   Boolean operators.

2. REPORT TEMPLATES: Admins need to create report templates that are available
   to staff. Templates should be runnable as-is or modified. Changes shouldn't
   compromise results. Admins should be able to limit which filters and display
   fields can be altered.

   Example: Front-line staff can set a call number range for a weeding report
   or add/remove display fields from a pick list, but can't alter the template
   to display deleted items.

3. PERMISSIONS: We need distinct, fine-grained permission levels limiting who
   can create and clone reports. Admins can create shared folders to allow or
   disallow staff from running specific reports, and/or to run ad hoc reports
   on specific sets of data.

4. BOARD REPORTS: Pre-defined reports for library boards with basic statistics
   (Georgia Annual Report requirements). Activity reports showing traffic and
   volume of use - checkouts, check-ins, holds placed, holds filled. Cross-
   tabulated per terminal, per branch, per system, per hour, per age range,
   per patron type, per patron location.

5. TRANSACTION ARCHIVE: Transactions archived protecting patron privacy per
   State Law, while providing useful demographic statistics.

6. QUERY SELECTIONS: System provides query selections along with results.

7. REPORTS QUEUING: Ability to see where your report is in the queue.

Jenny
===
From: susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org
To: jennifer.durham@statesboro.lib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: RE: Report features and interface requirements
Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2009 10:15:00 -0500

Jenny, this is great. Let me add some details about the report templates feature:

The key benefit of templates is consistency. We want to make sure that when
the director asks for "the weeding report," everyone runs the same report with
the same criteria. Templates ensure this.

We also need the ability to "clone" reports - take an existing template and
create a new one based on it. This is different from modifying the template -
it's creating a new variant.

The permissions need to be easy to administer. If I change someone from "Staff"
to "Manager," their report permissions should update automatically based on
the role.

- Susan
===
From: dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org
To: jennifer.durham@statesboro.lib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: RE: Report features and interface requirements
Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2009 11:45:00 -0500

One more thing on report queuing - staff get frustrated when they submit a
report and never hear back. They need to see:
- That their report is in the queue
- How many reports are ahead of theirs
- When their report was submitted
- Status (waiting, running, completed, failed)

Also, for the transaction archive - we need this for compliance. State law
requires us to retain transaction data for X years, but patron privacy means
we can't keep personally identifiable information.

Dana
===
From: george.tuttle@piedmontlib.org
To: jennifer.durham@statesboro.lib.org, susansexton-cooley@saraboblib.org, dana.peeler@ohoopeelib.org, pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: RE: Report features and interface requirements
Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2009 14:20:00 -0500

I can confirm the importance of report queuing from the IT side. Without
queue visibility, staff call the help desk thinking reports are "broken"
when they're just waiting in line. A visible queue would reduce these calls
significantly.

Also, the ability to prioritize certain reports is crucial. A director's
board report should be able to jump ahead of a staff member's ad-hoc query.

George
===
From: katherine.gregory@gapubliclib.org
To: pines-reports-working-group@gapl.org
Subject: SUMMARY: Report features thread
Date: Tue, 28 Jul 2009 09:00:00 -0500

Consolidating the report features discussion:

1. QUERY TOOL: User-friendly interface for designing queries against all record
   types. Boolean operators, picklists, regex support. Admin controls access.

2. REPORT TEMPLATES: Admins create templates available to staff. Run as-is or
   modified. Limit alterable filters/fields. Clone capability.

3. REPORTS PERMISSIONS: Fine-grained permission levels. Shared folders. Easy
   administration through roles.

4. BOARD REPORTS: Pre-defined reports for boards. Cross-tabulated per
   terminal/branch/system/hour/age/patron type/location.

5. TRANSACTION ARCHIVE: Archive with privacy protection per State Law.

6. QUERY SELECTIONS: Show criteria with results.

7. REPORTS QUEUING: See position in queue, status, priority.

8. PRIORITY: Important reports can jump queue.

These are all being added to the requirements matrix.

- Katherine"

}

messages.content:
You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

 "document": {
  "id": "D15",
  "path": "interview_cataloging_2009-05-08.txt",
  "text": "================================================================================
PINES REPORTS WORKING GROUP - INTERVIEW RECORD
================================================================================

Interview Date: May 8, 2009
Interviewer: Jennifer Durham, Statesboro Regional Library System
Interview Duration: 50 minutes
Location: Augusta-Reed Branch Library, Staff Meeting Room
Format: Semi-structured interview

INTERVIEWEE:
Name: Thomas Wright
Title: Senior Cataloger, Augusta-Reed Branch Library
Years in librarianship: 8
PINES experience: 4 years
Responsibilities: Cataloging, collection development, weeding, data quality

PURPOSE OF INTERVIEW:
To gather requirements for the PINES Reports Working Group from the perspective
of cataloging and collection management staff.

================================================================================
TRANSCRIPT
================================================================================

JENNIFER: Thomas, thanks for meeting with me. Let's start with your daily work.
What kind of reporting needs do you have in cataloging?

THOMAS: Well, one big area is uncataloged material. At Augusta-Reed, we get
large shipments of paperback books and children's board books that arrive
without individual catalog records. We need to be able to track these as
inventory even though they're not fully cataloged.

The requirements are: quick distribution (we need to process these fast),
minimal branch labor (we can't spend a lot of time per item), and ability to
identify how the material is being used. We also need to count transactions
and include them in circulation statistics and reports.

JENNIFER: That sounds like a significant workflow. What about transfers between
branches?

THOMAS: Yes, the item transfer utility is crucial for us. We often need to
move batches of items between branches - for example, sending books to a mobile
library unit or to an outreach program collection. The utility needs several
capabilities:

First, we need to query for candidate materials. Maybe we want all items in
the children's section that haven't circulated in 6 months. Second, we need to
save these queries for repeated use - we do this monthly. Third, we need to
manually select titles from query results if we want to be more targeted.

Fourth, we need to change records of selected items to move them to a new
location. And there should be mechanisms for reverting items back to their
original location after a set period of time - like when a mobile library
returns to base.

JENNIFER: What about reporting on missing and damaged items?

THOMAS: We do monthly shelf reading and mark items as missing. I need a report
that shows all missing and damaged items per branch. This helps me track
collection health and identify patterns - if the same shelf always has missing
items, we might need to relocate it.

I also need the in-transit items report. When items are being transferred
between branches, they sometimes get lost. The report should show items that
have been in-transit for more than X days (configurable), per branch and per
system. It should merge the transit-to and transit-from into one report for
ease of use.

JENNIFER: Let me ask about weeding and purging. What reports do you need there?

THOMAS: Weeding reports are my most-used report type. I need to identify items
for purging based on customizable criteria. For example:
- Item has been in status "missing" for more than X months
- Item has status "discard/weed"

We also need a report to assist in converting items from one status to another.
Sometimes I need to change 100 items from "missing" to "discard/weed" in batch.

And the last copy report is CRITICAL. This singles out a library system's last
copies, to assist catalogers who need to edit WorldCat entries. Last month, we
almost deleted our last copy of a rare book before someone remembered to check
WorldCat. If we had a report like this, it would save us from that situation.

There also needs to be a quick, effective method for deleting volume entries
along with copy entries, as well as records with no items attached. Right now,
cleaning up these orphaned records takes forever.

JENNIFER: What about tracking deletions?

THOMAS: Yes, we need to count and track record deletions per location and per
system. This is important for auditing - our directors want to know how many
records we've deleted and why. It also helps with troubleshooting if something
goes missing from the catalog.

JENNIFER: Any other cataloging-specific requirements?

THOMAS: Yes, a few:

1. The shelf space report is important for collection management. For each
   genre and format, I need to compare:
   - Percentage of total circulations
   - Percentage of the collection
   - Percentage of total shelf space
   This helps me decide where to allocate resources.

2. The material volume report helps me understand how much we have. I need to
   report on volume based on acquisitions, items on shelf, and items in
   circulation, broken down by categories like total items, holds, adult
   fiction, board books, etc.

3. Data quality reports - items with invalid item type, items with long call
   numbers, bibliographic records with no item records. These help me maintain
   data integrity.

4. I need to be able to see the last edit date on reports, but it should be
   only when the item is edited and not include the last circulation. The
   current system combines these dates.

JENNIFER: Thank you, Thomas. This has been very detailed and helpful.

INTERVIEWER'S NOTES:
- Thomas provided very specific, actionable requirements
- He emphasized the importance of batch operations and data quality
- The last copy report and WorldCat integration are critical
- He mentioned several requirements that overlap with other interviews,
  confirming their validity

COMPLETED BY: Jennifer Durham
DATE: May 10, 2009"
 }
}

candidates.name: Track Uncataloged Materials
candidates.description: The system must track uncataloged paperback books, children's board books, and other material as inventory before individual catalog records are available, while supporting rapid distribution with minimal branch labor and enabling staff to identify how the material is being used.

candidates.name: Count Uncataloged Transactions
candidates.description: The system must count transactions involving uncataloged material and include those transactions in circulation statistics and reports.

candidates.name: Query Transfer Candidates
candidates.description: The item transfer utility must allow staff to query for candidate materials, such as all items in the children's section that have not circulated in six months, for transfer between branches or to mobile and outreach collections.

candidates.name: Save Transfer Queries
candidates.description: The item transfer utility must allow staff to save candidate-material queries for repeated use, including monthly reuse.

candidates.name: Select Transfer Items
candidates.description: The item transfer utility must allow staff to manually select individual titles from query results when a targeted transfer is required.

candidates.name: Change Item Locations
candidates.description: The item transfer utility must allow staff to change the records of selected items so that the items move to a new location.

candidates.name: Revert Item Locations
candidates.description: The item transfer utility must provide a mechanism to return transferred items to their original location after a defined period, such as when a mobile library returns to its base.

candidates.name: Report Missing Damaged Items
candidates.description: The system must provide a report showing all missing and damaged items for each branch so collection management staff can monitor collection health and identify patterns of loss or damage.

candidates.name: Report Overdue Transit Items
candidates.description: The system must provide one report combining transit-to and transit-from items that have remained in transit longer than a configurable number of days, with results available per branch and for the entire system.

candidates.name: Identify Purge Candidates
candidates.description: The system must provide a weeding report that identifies items for purging using customizable criteria, including items that have been in status "missing" longer than a specified number of months and items with status "discard/weed."

candidates.name: Batch Change Item Status
candidates.description: The system must provide a report or operation that assists staff in converting selected items from one status to another in batch, including changing 100 items from "missing" to "discard/weed."

candidates.name: Report Last System Copies
candidates.description: The system must provide a report identifying the last copies held by a library system so catalogers can check and edit corresponding WorldCat entries before deleting or otherwise altering a rare or final copy.

candidates.name: Delete Orphaned Records
candidates.description: The system must provide a quick, effective method for deleting volume entries together with their copy entries and for deleting records that have no items attached, to support cleanup of orphaned catalog records.

candidates.name: Track Record Deletions
candidates.description: The system must count and track record deletions by location and by library system, including the reason for each deletion, to support auditing and troubleshooting.

candidates.name: Report Shelf Space Allocation
candidates.description: The system must provide a shelf space report that compares, for each genre and format, the percentage of total circulations, the percentage of the collection, and the percentage of total shelf space, so collection managers can allocate resources.

candidates.name: Report Material Volumes
candidates.description: The system must provide a material volume report covering acquisitions, items on shelf, and items in circulation, broken down by categories such as total items, holds, adult fiction, and board books.

candidates.name: Provide Data Quality Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide data quality reports identifying items with invalid item types, items with excessively long call numbers, and bibliographic records with no item records, so staff can maintain catalog data integrity.

candidates.name: Display Item Edit Dates
candidates.description: Reports must show the date an item was last edited, where the date changes only when the item is edited and does not treat the last circulation as an edit; the edit date must not be combined with the last circulation date.

outputs.name: Change Item Locations
outputs.description: The item transfer utility must allow staff to change the records of selected items so that the items move to a new location.

outputs.name: Revert Item Locations
outputs.description: The item transfer utility must provide a mechanism to return transferred items to their original location after a defined period, such as when a mobile library returns to its base.

outputs.name: Report Missing Damaged Items
outputs.description: The system must provide a report showing all missing and damaged items for each branch so collection management staff can monitor collection health and identify patterns of loss or damage.

outputs.name: Report Overdue Transit Items
outputs.description: The system must provide one report combining transit-to and transit-from items that have remained in transit longer than a configurable number of days, with results available per branch and for the entire system.

outputs.name: Identify Purge Candidates
outputs.description: The system must provide a weeding report that identifies items for purging using customizable criteria, including items that have been in status "missing" longer than a specified number of months and items with status "discard/weed."

outputs.name: Batch Change Item Status
outputs.description: The system must provide a report or operation that assists staff in converting selected items from one status to another in batch, including changing 100 items from "missing" to "discard/weed."

outputs.name: Report Last System Copies
outputs.description: The system must provide a report identifying the last copies held by a library system so catalogers can check and edit corresponding WorldCat entries before deleting or otherwise altering a rare or final copy.
outputs.source_priority_note: D15 marks the last copy report as critical

outputs.name: Delete Orphaned Records
outputs.description: The system must provide a quick, effective method for deleting volume entries together with their copy entries and for deleting records that have no items attached, to support cleanup of orphaned catalog records.

outputs.name: Track Record Deletions
outputs.description: The system must count and track record deletions by location and by library system, including the reason for each deletion, to support auditing and troubleshooting.

outputs.name: Report Shelf Space Allocation
outputs.description: The system must provide a shelf space report that compares, for each genre and format, the percentage of total circulations, the percentage of the collection, and the percentage of total shelf space, so collection managers can allocate resources.

outputs.name: Report Material Volumes
outputs.description: The system must provide a material volume report covering acquisitions, items on shelf, and items in circulation, broken down by categories such as total items, holds, adult fiction, and board books.

outputs.name: Provide Data Quality Reports
outputs.description: The system must provide data quality reports identifying items with invalid item types, items with excessively long call numbers, and bibliographic records with no item records, so staff can maintain catalog data integrity.

outputs.name: Display Item Edit Dates
outputs.description: Reports must show the date an item was last edited, where the date changes only when the item is edited and does not treat the last circulation as an edit; the edit date must not be combined with the last circulation date.

  "text": "================================================================================
PINES REPORTS WORKING GROUP - INTERVIEW RECORD
================================================================================

Interview Date: May 10, 2009
Interviewer: George Tuttle, Piedmont Regional Library
Interview Duration: 55 minutes
Location: PINES Central Office, IT Department Conference Room
Format: Semi-structured interview

INTERVIEWEE:
Name: Robert Chen
Title: Senior Systems Administrator, PINES IT Department
Years in IT: 15
PINES experience: 3 years
Technical expertise: Linux systems, PostgreSQL, network infrastructure,
                     accessibility compliance

PURPOSE OF INTERVIEW:
To gather technical requirements for the Management Processes reporting system,
including server environment, browser requirements, accessibility compliance,
database architecture, and user permissions management.

================================================================================
TRANSCRIPT
================================================================================

GEORGE: Robert, thanks for taking the time to meet with me. Let's start with the
server environment. What are the current server specifications for PINES?

ROBERT: Our main server is a Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5 box with dual quad-core
processors and 32GB of RAM. It runs PostgreSQL 8.3 for the database. We also
have a secondary site that runs Solaris 10 on SPARC hardware for disaster
recovery and reporting. So any reporting system needs to work on both Linux
and Solaris.

GEORGE: Do you anticipate any issues with report processing during peak hours?

ROBERT: That's actually a major concern. Right now, when someone runs a complex
report, it can tie up the database and slow down the circulation client. We
need to make sure reports can be queued and processed in the background. Or we
need read-only reporting replicas. The key requirement is that searches and
reports can be processed during open hours without disrupting other system
functions.

GEORGE: What about browser requirements? Which browsers do libraries use?

ROBERT: It's a mixed bag. Most of our libraries standardize on Microsoft
Internet Explorer, but many have moved to Firefox. IE 6 is still common in
our environment - I know it's old, but upgrading browsers on 200+ library
computers is expensive and time-consuming. Firefox 2.0 is also still in use
at some locations. So we need to support IE 6.0+ and Firefox 2.0+.

GEORGE: Any thoughts on accessibility requirements?

ROBERTY: This is non-negotiable. As a public institution, we MUST comply with
Section 508 accessibility requirements. The system needs to work with:
  - Screen readers like JAWS and NVDA
  - Screen magnification software like ZoomText
  - Other assistive technology programs

We can't have blind staff members unable to run reports. The HTML output
needs to be properly structured with alt tags, ARIA labels, and proper
semantic HTML. And the system needs to produce standards-compliant HTML.

GEORGE: What about the database architecture?

ROBERT: We're using PostgreSQL now, which is a fully relational database.
That's good - it means we can write complex joins. The reporting system needs
to work with the relational structure, not fight against it. Some systems try
to use denormalized reporting schemas, but that creates sync issues. I'd
prefer to keep everything in the main relational database.

GEORGE: How do you manage user permissions currently?

ROBERT: PINES uses a role-based system. We have different levels of access:
  - Patron (public access through OPAC)
  - Staff (basic circulation functions)
  - Local Admin (branch manager - can run reports, configure local settings)
  - Global Admin (IT staff - full system access)

The permission system needs to be controlled through security groups and/or
"roles." This allows access control for individuals, workgroups, and arbitrary
staff groups. The system needs to make it easy to administer these roles.
Changing someone's permissions should be a simple matter of changing their
role assignment.

GEORGE: What about development and training environments?

ROBERT: We definitely need separate environments. Developers need a place to
test new reports without affecting production. And new staff members need a
training environment where they can practice running reports without worrying
about making mistakes.

The key is that configurations developed in training/dev need to be migratable
to production. We need export/import functionality for report templates,
permission settings, and other configuration.

GEORGE: Any other technical requirements?

ROBERT: Yes - the OPAC module. The management reporting system must not
constrain the OPAC in any way. These are separate concerns. Patrons need
fast, responsive access to the catalog. If the reporting system is doing a
big query, it should NOT slow down the OPAC.

Also, the help system needs to be online, hierarchical, and cross-linked.
Staff shouldn't have to call IT every time they want to know how to run a
report. The HTML help needs to be searchable and easy to navigate.

GEORGE: Thank you, Robert. This has been very informative.

INTERVIEWER'S NOTES:
- Robert's technical perspective confirms many requirements from other sources
- Server environment (Linux/Solaris) is validated
- Browser requirements (IE/Firefox) confirmed
- Accessibility is not just a nice-to-have - it's a legal requirement
- Database architecture needs are clear (relational, PostgreSQL-compatible)
- Role-based access control is confirmed as essential
- Separation of reporting from OPAC is critical
- Development/training environments with migration capability needed

COMPLETED BY: George Tuttle
DATE: May 12, 2009"

}

PINES REPORTS WORKING GROUP - FIRST MEETING MINUTES
================================================================================

Date: March 15, 2009
Time: 10:00 AM - 12:30 PM EST
Location: Georgia Public Library Service, Conference Room B, Atlanta, GA
Meeting Type: Organizational / Planning

ATTENDEES:
- Katherine Gregory (PINES Services Specialist) - Chair
- LaToya Davidson (Twin Lakes Library System) - Library Director
- Jennifer Durham (Statesboro Regional Library System) - Assistant Library Director
- Dana Peeler (Ohoopee Regional Library) - Systems Librarian
- Susan Sexton-Cooley (Sara Hightower Regional Library) - Assistant Library Director
- George Tuttle (Piedmont Regional Library) - Assistant Library Director

APPROVAL OF AGENDA:
The agenda was approved as circulated.

1. CALL TO ORDER AND INTRODUCTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine Gregory called the meeting to order at 10:05 AM. She introduced
herself as the facilitator for the Reports Working Group. She noted that this
group was formed in late February 2009 following discussions at the PINES
Annual Conference about difficulties library staff were experiencing with the
current reports interface in Evergreen.

Katherine explained that King County Library System (WA) had previously worked
with Galecia Group to develop a comprehensive Software Requirements Specification
for a reports interface. PINES staff decided to use that as a foundation and
adapt it for our specific needs. She mentioned that Lori Ayre and Lucien Kress
from Galecia Group had been contacted and were willing to share their draft.

2. FORMATION AND MISSION DISCUSSION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dana Peeler moved to adopt the following mission statement for the working
group. The motion was seconded by Susan Sexton-Cooley and carried unanimously:

  "Reports Working Group Mission:
   - Document optimal Reports functionality within a future Evergreen release
     and develop a list of requirements.
   - Become the Reports testing group, through which all new Reports development
     would be filtered.
   - Compile a list of reports needed for an Executive Reports Interface.
   - Determine and create templates needed for all PINES libraries."

3. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Jennifer Durham asked about the scope of the group's work. Katherine explained
that the group would focus on Management Processes - that is, reports and
analysis tools used by library managers, administrators, and staff for
planning, evaluation, and oversight purposes. She clarified that this does NOT
include day-to-day patron-facing functions (those are part of the OPAC and
circulation client).

The following scope items were identified:

  - Analyzing the Library collection and its use by patrons
  - Analyzing branch capacity and optimal distribution of the collection
  - Analyzing demographics and interests of patrons
  - Analyzing staff productivity and workflow
  - Tracking and verifying financial transactions

Susan Sexton-Cooley noted that the current specification presupposes the
general data structures and functionality of a full-fledged ILS. She said
PINES is currently working on separate specifications for Acquisitions and
Cataloging modules. The group agreed to specify only those requirements that
directly or indirectly relate to management activities.

Dana Peeler raised the question of user interface specification. Katherine
noted that while UI would eventually need detailed specification, for now the
focus should be on functional requirements. She mentioned that UI and data
structures would require further specification using an iterative, prototype-
oriented methodology.

4. USER CLASSES AND CHARACTERISTICS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The group discussed the different types of users who would interact with
Management Processes:

  Patron: A resident of the State of Georgia, either possessing a library card
          or not, utilizing the resources of a PINES member library.
          [Note from Katherine: Patrons interact through OPAC; they may use
          reports indirectly through displays/screens at libraries]

  Staff: Paid employees of PINES member libraries involved in designing and
         providing services. This includes front-line circulation staff,
         supervisors, etc.
         [Jenny: Staff are our primary content creators for reports]

  Local System Administrators: Management staff who oversee Library processes.
                                They configure the system locally.
                                [Susan: These are branch managers / assistant
                                directors]

  Library Managers: Supervise a single organizational unit and provide input to
                   design and implementation of Library services.
                   [LaToya: Directors and assistant directors in this role]

  Library Directors: Members of the Library Executive Team who plan and direct
                     Library services and priorities.
                     [George: These are our board-level stakeholders]

  Global System Administrator: Manages PINES at the consortium level,
                               implementing software changes and configurations,
                               and generating statistical reports for PINES as
                               a whole.
                               [Katherine: This is the PINES central IT team]

5. INTENDED AUDIENCE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine stated that this SRS would be intended both for library managers and
staff who may contribute additional requirements, and for software project
managers and developers who will implement the requirements. She emphasized
the need to aim for a high level of readability for a non-technical audience
while providing enough specificity for developers.

The group discussed the development approach. It was noted that development
would likely happen in a highly collaborative and iterative environment where
end-users have multiple opportunities to review prototypes. It was assumed that
readers have a general understanding of Library services and processes and
do not require definition of common Library terminology.

6. NEXT STEPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine assigned the following action items:

  - Each member will conduct at least one interview with staff at their library
    system to gather report needs (due by April 15, 2009)
  - Katherine will circulate the King County / Galecia Group draft for reference
  - A follow-up meeting is scheduled for July 20, 2009 to review findings
  - A technical subcommittee meeting will be held in late June to discuss
    architectural constraints

Meeting adjurned at 12:25 PM.

Minutes prepared by: Katherine Gregory, PINES Services Specialist
Minutes distributed: March 17, 2009"

messages.content:
You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

  "text": "================================================================================
EVERGREEN ILS - REPORTING MODULE OVERVIEW
================================================================================
Reference Document
Version: 1.4.0.4
Date: March 15, 2009
Source: Evergreen Official Documentation & PINES IT Department Analysis

================================================================================
1. SYSTEM OVERVIEW
================================================================================

Evergreen is an open-source Integrated Library System (ILS) originally
developed by the Georgia Public Library Service for use in PINES. The current
version in production at PINES is 1.4.0.4.

This document provides an overview of the existing reporting capabilities
within Evergreen, along with identified gaps and limitations that have driven
the need for enhanced Management Processes reporting.

PINES currently operates Evergreen across 286 library locations, serving
approximately 3.5 million patrons with a collection of 9.6 million items.

================================================================================
2. EXISTING REPORTING COMPONENTS
================================================================================

2.1 REPORT WRITER INTERFACE
Evergreen includes a report writer that allows staff to create custom reports
using a web-based interface. Key features:

- Drag-and-drop field selection
- Basic filtering and sorting
- Multiple output formats (CSV, HTML, sometimes Excel)
- Ability to save and reuse report definitions

Limitations:
- Complex queries are difficult to construct
- No Boolean operators (AND/OR) beyond simple filters
- Limited field selection (not all database fields are available)
- No regular expression support
- No query queue visibility

2.2 CANNED REPORTS
Pre-defined reports available in Evergreen 1.4.0.4:

CIRCULATION:
- Checkout Count
- Renewals Count
- Non-Cataloged Count
- Circulation Count by Shelving Location

ITEMS:
- Items Added Count
- Items Deleted Count
- Items Currently Checked Out
- Items Overdue by X Days
- List of Items with Missing Status

BIB RECORDS:
- Bib Records Count
- Bib Records with No Volumes Attached

PATRONS:
- Patron Count
- Patron Count by Home Library

BILLS:
- Bills Currently Owed by Patrons
- Detailed Payments Received
- Aged Debt

2.3 REPORT SCHEDULING
Some reports can be scheduled to run at regular intervals (daily, weekly,
monthly). However, scheduling options are limited:

- No hourly scheduling
- No ability to check multiple reports to run at the same time
- No email delivery (reports can only be downloaded from the web interface)

2.4 PERMISSIONS
Current permission model:
- Staff can run any report they can access
- No fine-grained control over who can create vs. run reports
- No shared folders concept
- No ability to limit which filters staff can use

================================================================================
3. REPORTABLE DATA STRUCTURES
================================================================================

3.1 RECORD TYPES
The following record types are available for reporting:

- bibliographic_record: Title, author, ISBN, publication info, subjects, etc.
- item: Call number, barcode, location (copy location), status, etc.
- patron: Name, address, library, patron type, etc.
- action_circulation: Checkout, checkout, renewal, holds, etc.
- action_hold: Hold requests
- money: Fines, payments, credits, etc.
- actor: Staff accounts and permissions

3.2 KEY RELATIONSHIPS
- bibliographic_record -> item (through asset.copy)
- item -> action.circulation (through circulation transactions)
- patron -> action.circulation (through patron_id)
- patron -> money (through debt records)
- actor -> action.circulation (through librarian link)

3.3 AVAILABLE FIELDS (SAMPLE)
For bibliographic_record:
- id, fingerprint, scan_timestamp, record_type,
  edition, language, ISBN, ISSN, UPC, EAN, publisher_name,
  publication_date, place_of_publication, physical_description

For item:
- id, barcode, label, copy_number, location (copy_location),
  status (acq status), circ_modifier, call_number,
  purchase_date, purchase_price, shelving_location,
  age_hold_protect, reserve_id

For patron:
- id, barcode, opac (visible fields), family_lib (home library),
  usr_grp (patron type), em (email),
  address lines, city, state, zip (postal code),
  birth_date, create_date

================================================================================
4. IDENTIFIED GAPS AND LIMITATIONS
================================================================================

The following reporting capabilities are MISSING from Evergreen 1.4.0.4 or
are severely limited:

4.1 MISSING REPORT TYPES
- Circulation Count by Circ Modifier (partially available)
- Circulation Count by Dewey (not available)
- Circulation Count by MARC fields (not available)
- Circulation Count by Circ Location broken down by Patron County (not available)
- Circulation Count by Age Demographic (not available)
- Items Edited Count (not available)
- List of Items by Fines Stopped Reason (not available)
- Items more than XX days overdue with patron contact info (not available)
- List of Items with specific Total Use Count (not available)
- Last Copy Report (partially available, needs enhancement)
- List of Items by Creation Date Range (not available)
- Claims Returned report (not available)
- Weeding report with date of last circulation (partially available)
- Age of collection by call number (not available)
- Price value of collection by call number (not available)
- Bib Records Edited Count (not available)
- Bib Records Added by user by library Count (not available)
- Bib Records missing specific MARC fields (not available)
- Patron Count by Age Demographic (not available)
- Patron Count by County (not available)
- Patron Count by County, City, & Zip Code (not available)
- Voter Survey Responses (not available)
- List of Patrons with inactive status (not available)
- Staff Accounts with date of last password change (not available)
- Holds Purchase Alert (not available)
- Unfilled Holds (not available)
- Stale Holds (not available)
- Aged Debt detailed report (partially available, needs enhancement)

4.2 MISSING FEATURES
- No report queue visibility (staff can't see where their report is in queue)
- No ability to prioritize certain types of reports
- No ability to cancel a running report
- No pivot table output
- No real-time reporting (all reports are run on current data)
- No historical reporting warehouse
- No ability to select Run ASAP, Hourly, Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Yearly
- No email delivery of reports
- No address book for report delivery
- No ability to upload text files for filtering (barcodes, TCNs)
- No selection criteria display in report results
- No ability to edit canned report display options
- No quick access interface with pop-up descriptions
- No hover tooltips for report titles

4.3 MISSING ARCHITECTURAL ELEMENTS
- No separate reporting database/replica (reports run on production database)
- No background processing for long-running reports
- No report template management system
- No fine-grained permissions for reports
- No development/training environment separation
- No configuration migration between environments
- No accessibility support for report interface
- No online help system integrated with reports

4.4 FINE-GRAINED REQUIREMENTS NOT MET
Several fine-grained reporting requirements from the King County specification
are not met by Evergreen 1.4.0.4:

- Three interfaces (canned, on-demand, open template) - only basic canned exists
- Open Template Reporting - does not exist
- Real time reporting - does not exist
- Historical reporting warehouse - does not exist
- Snapshot bills report going back in time - does not exist
- Last edit date not including last circulation - does not exist
- Ability to indicate last circulation date - not available as separate field
- Checkin Date/time not including renewals - checkin and renewal timestamps
  are stored together
- All nulls and blank fields included in results - current system may filter
  some nulls

================================================================================
5. CONCLUSION
================================================================================

Evergreen 1.4.0.4 provides basic reporting capabilities but has significant
gaps in several areas. The management processes reporting system needs to:

1. Expand the available report types to cover all identified gaps
2. Implement fine-grained permissions and template management
3. Add report queue visibility and status indicators
4. Provide multiple output formats and scheduling options
5. Implement accessibility compliance
6. Separate reporting from production operations
7. Provide a development/training environment with migration capability

This analysis was conducted by the PINES IT Department and is based on
review of the Evergreen codebase version 1.4.0.4 and production usage patterns
observed in the PINES environment.

================================================================================
END OF DOCUMENT
================================================================================"
 }
}
