messages.content:
You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

  "text": "================================================================================
PINES TECHNICAL SUBCOMMITTEE MEETING NOTES
================================================================================

Date: June 30, 2009
Time: 2:00 PM - 4:30 PM EST
Location: PINES Central Office, Server Room Conference Room
Meeting Type: Technical Subcommittee - Architecture Discussion

ATTENDEES:
- Katherine Gregory (PINES Services Specialist)
- Robert Chen (Senior Systems Administrator)
- Dana Peeler (Ohoopee Regional Library) - Systems Librarian
- George Tuttle (Piedmont Regional Library) - Assistant Director
- Chris Sharp (PINES Staff Facilitator)

NOTE TAKER: Chris Sharp

1. OPENING REMARKS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine opened the meeting, explaining that the technical subcommittee was
formed to discuss the architectural and implementation details of the Management
Processes reporting system. This meeting would focus on design constraints,
documentation requirements, and dependencies.

2. DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS - DETAILED DISCUSSION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Robert led the discussion on design constraints.

2.1 DATABASE CONSTRAINTS
Robert confirmed that the system must use a fully relational database back-end.
He noted that PostgreSQL is the current choice for PINES and it meets this
requirement. The reporting system must work WITH the relational structure,
not against it.

"I strongly recommend against denormalization for reporting," Robert said.
"Maintaining sync between a reporting warehouse and the live database creates
more problems than it solves. Modern SQL databases can handle complex analytical
queries if they're written properly."

2.2 HTML COMPLIANCE
The system must produce standards-compliant HTML. This was discussed in the
context of the web-based interface, the help system, and report output.

"We need to make sure all HTML output validates against W3C standards,"
Robert noted. "This isn't just about looks - it's about compatibility with
different browsers and assistive technologies."

2.3 DEVELOPMENT AND TRAINING ENVIRONMENT
The need for separate development, training, and production environments was
discussed.

"We have a dev server, a training server, and production," Robert explained.
"What we need is a way to migrate configurations between them. Export/import
of templates, permission settings, and saved queries."

Katherine added: "And the training environment needs to be safe - staff should
be able to experiment without risking production data."

2.4 USER RIGHTS AND ROLES
The role-based access control system was detailed:

Robert: "We need security groups and/or 'roles' that allow access control for
individuals, workgroups, and arbitrary staff groups. The system should make it
easy to change someone's permissions by simply changing their role assignment."

Key points:
- Global Admin: Full system access
- Local Admin: Branch-level reporting and configuration
- Library Manager: Run approved reports, limited template modification
- Staff: Run reports within assigned permissions
- Patron: Indirect access through OPAC displays

2.5 OPAC CONSTRAINTS
"We absolutely cannot constrain the OPAC," Robert emphasized. "The management
reporting system is separate from the public catalog. If a report is running,
it should not slow down the OPAC."

3. USER DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This section was led by Katherine.

3.1 DATA SPECIFICATIONS
The developer must provide complete data specifications for:
- Authority records
- Bibliographic records
- Order records
- Item records
- Hold/request records
- Other records maintained or accessed by Management Processes

Katherine: "Staff need to understand the data structures to write effective
queries. We need data dictionaries - field names, data types, relationships."

3.2 PROCESS DESCRIPTIONS
The developer must provide a thorough high-level description of major processes,
including:
- Bibliographic record import and export
- Validation of bibliographic records against internal and external authority
  sources
- Standard reports

3.3 ONLINE HELP SYSTEM
The system shall provide an online, hierarchical, and cross-linked help system
in HTML.

Robert: "This has to be accessible too. The help system needs to work with
screen readers."

3.4 ERROR REPORTING
The system shall provide thorough high-level error reporting and feedback,
and shall allow low-level query-specific feedback for administrators.

"When a report fails, we need to know WHY," Robert said. "Generic error messages
like 'query failed' are useless. We need specifics - which table, which field,
what kind of error."

4. ASSUMPTIONS AND DEPENDENCIES - TECHNICAL PERSPECTIVE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.1 ENTERPRISE-LEVEL SYSTEM
AS-1: Management Processes are part of an enterprise-level Library Automation
System.

Robert: "This means we can rely on the infrastructure - redundant servers,
backup systems, network connectivity."

4.2 CENTRAL CONSOLIDATION
AS-2: Management Processes are consolidated at a central location, and accept
input and provide services to multiple locations.

"Centralization is good for reporting," Katherine noted. "We get a single
source of truth. The challenge is making sure data from all locations is complete
and current."

4.3 LIBRARY AUTOMATION DEPENDENCIES
DE-1: Management Processes rely on the data structures and functionality of
an enterprise-level Library Automation System, including Acquisitions and
Cataloging modules.

"All our data comes from the ILS," Robert said. "The reporting system doesn't
manage acquisitions or cataloging - it just reads the data."

4.4 VENDOR INTEGRATION
DE-2: Management Processes interface with a variety of vendor websites, via
published APIs and/or automated transfer of standard-format data files
(e.g., USMARC21, EDIFACT).

"We have some vendors that provide EDI ordering data," Robert explained.
"The reporting system needs to handle this data, but we can't rely on it
being present at every library."

4.5 OPAC INTEGRATION
DE-3: Management Processes interact with a patron interface (OPAC).

"Patrons create holds and circulation transactions through the OPAC," Robert
said. "The reporting system queries this data, but doesn't modify it."

5. FINE-GRAINED REPORTING REQUIREMENTS - TECHNICAL DETAILS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The technical feasibility of several fine-grained requirements was discussed:

5.1 OUTPUT FORMATS
Excel, HTML, and CSV formats are required. Robert noted that CSV is the most
reliable for data export, Excel is preferred by business users for pivot tables,
and HTML is needed for web display.

5.2 REAL-TIME vs HISTORICAL REPORTING
"Some reports need to be real-time - like 'what's overdue today,'" Robert said.
"Others are historical - 'what was the bill amount on June 30th?' We probably
need a reporting warehouse for historical data."

5.3 REPORT CANCELLATION
The ability to cancel a scheduled or running report is technically feasible,
but requires the system to check for cancellation signals during report
processing.

5.4 NULL HANDLING
"All nulls and blank fields must be included in the results," Robert noted.
"This is actually the default behavior in SQL, but we need to make sure it's
explicitly required."

5.5 SURVEY FILTERING
The ability to filter by survey name rather than survey ID requires the system
to resolve names to IDs internally.

6. ACTION ITEMS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - Robert to research reporting warehouse options for historical data
  - Katherine to compile technical requirements document
  - George to draft the architecture overview section
  - All attendees to review the fine-grained requirements for technical
    feasibility
  - Follow-up technical meeting scheduled for August 15, 2009

Meeting adjourned at 4:25 PM.

Notes prepared by: Chris Sharp
Notes distributed: July 2, 2009"
 }
}

- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

PINES REPORTS WORKING GROUP - SECOND MEETING MINUTES
================================================================================

Date: July 20, 2009
Time: 9:30 AM - 12:00 PM EST
Location: Georgia Public Library Service, Conference Room A, Atlanta, GA
Meeting Type: Regular Working Group Meeting

ATTENDEES:
- Katherine Gregory (PINES Services Specialist) - Chair
- LaToya Davidson (Twin Lakes Library System) - Library Director
- Jennifer Durham (Statesboro Regional Library System) - Assistant Library Director
- Dana Peeler (Ohoopee Regional Library) - Systems Librarian
- Susan Sexton-Cooley (Sara Hightower Regional Library) - Assistant Library Director
- George Tuttle (Piedmont Regional Library) - Assistant Library Director
- Chris Sharp (PINES Staff Facilitator)

ABSENTEES: None

1. CALL TO ORDER AND REVIEW OF ACTION ITEMS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine called the meeting to order at 9:35 AM.

Action items from the March 15 meeting:
  - Interviews with staff: COMPLETED (all members submitted reports)
  - Circulation of Galecia Group draft: COMPLETED
  - Technical subcommittee meeting: SCHEDULED for June 30 (see below)

2. INTERVIEW FINDINGS SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Each member presented a summary of their interview findings:

LaToya Davidson (Twin Lakes): Spoke with 3 branch managers. Key themes:
  - Inventory and capacity reports are used daily
  - Financial report needs are understood at the director level
  - Need for cross-branch comparison reports

Jennifer Durham (Statesboro): Spoke with 2 branch managers and 1 director.
  Key themes:
  - Report queue visibility is important
  - Board/executive reports need to be pre-defined
  - Data quality reports are needed

Dana Peeler (Ohoopee): Spoke with 1 branch manager. Key themes:
  - Staff login needs (card swipe) - already discussed via email
  - In-transit item reports are critical for delivery coordination
  - Missing/damaged item reports are needed per branch

Susan Sexton-Cooley (Sara Hightower): Spoke with 1 branch manager. Key themes:
  - Weeding reports are frequently used
  - Shelf space utilization reports are important
  - Demographic analysis for program planning

George Tuttle (Piedmont): Spoke with 1 branch manager and 1 IT staff.
  Key themes:
  - Technical constraints (server OS, browser support)
  - User permissions and role-based access
  - Accessibility requirements

3. OPERATING ENVIRONMENT REQUIREMENTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This section was led by Dana Peeler and George Tuttle, drawing on input from
their interviews.

OE-1: Management Processes must support the needs of a large, multiple-system
      library consortium. Specifically, the system must support a library
      consortium with 286 locations, 17 million annual circulations,
      purchasing and processing over 900,000 items per year. It is highly
      desirable that searches and reports can be processed during open hours
      without disrupting other system functions.

      [Discussion: George noted that Evergreen already handles this scale.
      The concern is about report processing during peak hours. We need
      background processing/queuing to prevent report generation from slowing
      down the circulation client.]

OE-2: Management Processes shall operate on a Linux or Solaris server.
      [Consensus: Both Linux and Solaris are acceptable. Most PINES
      installations use Linux, but some larger systems use Solaris.]

OE-3: Management Processes shall be accessible through a web-browser or a
      Windows-compatible client.
      [Discussion: This is critical - some libraries prefer browser-based
      access (no client install), others prefer the dedicated client for
      better performance.]

OE-4: If web-browser based, Management Processes shall be accessible through
      Microsoft Internet Explorer (v.6.0 and later) and Mozilla Firefox
      (v.2.0 and later).
      [Discussion: We need to support both IE and Firefox because different
      libraries standardize on different browsers. IE 6 is still common in
      our library environments, even though it's old.]

OE-5: Management Processes shall be accessible with screen-reading software,
      screen-magnification software, and other software programs designed to
      increase accessibility.
      [Discussion: Susan emphasized this is a legal requirement for public
      institutions. We need to support JAWS, NVDA, ZoomText, and other
      assistive technologies. Section 508 compliance is mandatory.]

4. DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This section was led by George Tuttle, drawing on his IT interview.

CO-1: Management Processes shall use a fully relational database back-end.
      [Discussion: Evergreen already uses PostgreSQL. We need to ensure our
      reporting layer works properly with the relational structure.]

CO-2: Management Processes shall produce standards-compliant HTML.
      [Discussion: All web output needs to be valid HTML. This affects report
      display, help system, and any web-based UI components.]

CO-3: Management Processes shall provide a development and training environment
      with the ability to migrate configurations to a production environment.
      [Discussion: Katherine noted that Evergreen development follows this
      pattern - developers have separate environments. We need to make sure
      report templates and configurations can be exported/imported.]

CO-4: User rights and privileges will be controlled through security groups
      and/or "roles" that allow access control for individuals, workgroups,
      and arbitrary staff groups.
      [Discussion: George confirmed this is essential. We need flexible
      role-based access control.]

CO-5: These requirements shall not constrain functionality or features of the
      Online Public Access Catalog (OPAC) module.
      [Discussion: The management processes are separate from the public-
      facing catalog. Changes to management reporting should not affect
      patron access.]

5. USER DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine led a discussion on user documentation needs:

UD-1: The software developer shall provide complete data specifications for
      authority records, bibliographic records, order records, item records,
      hold/request records, and other records maintained or accessed by
      Management Processes.

      [Discussion: Staff need to understand the data structures to write
      effective queries. Data dictionaries are essential.]

UD-2: The software developer shall provide a thorough high-level description
      of major processes, including bibliographic record import and export,
      validation of bibliographic records against internal and external
      authority sources, and standard reports.

      [Discussion: Process flow documentation helps staff understand how
      data moves through the system.]

UD-3: The system shall provide an online, hierarchical, and cross-linked help
      system in HTML that describes and illustrates all system functions.

      [Discussion: Context-sensitive help is critical. Staff shouldn't have
      to leave the system to find documentation.]

UD-4: The system shall provide thorough high-level error reporting and feedback
      and shall allow low-level query-specific feedback for Local and Global
      System Administrators from the front-end interface.

      [Discussion: When reports fail, staff need to understand why. Error
      messages should be meaningful.]

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND DEPENDENCIES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
AS-1: Management Processes are part of an enterprise-level Library Automation
      System.
      [Discussion: This means we can rely on the infrastructure being
      enterprise-grade. Evergreen is that system for PINES.]

AS-2: Management Processes are consolidated at a central location, and accept
      input and provide services to multiple locations.
      [Discussion: Centralization enables consistent reporting but requires
      good network connectivity.]

DE-1: Management Processes rely on the data structures and functionality of an
      enterprise-level Library Automation System, including Acquisitions and
      Cataloging modules.
      [Discussion: The data we report on comes from the ILS. We don't manage
      acquisitions or cataloging ourselves.]

DE-2: Management Processes interface with a variety of vendor websites, via
      published APIs and/or automated transfer of standard-format data files
      (e.g., USMARC21, EDIFACT).
      [Discussion: Some libraries use external vendors for certain functions.
      Our reporting needs to handle data from these sources too.]

DE-3: Management Processes interact with a patron interface, also known as an
      Online Public Access Catalog (OPAC).
      [Discussion: Patron data (holds, circulation) is created in the OPAC.
      Our reports need to query this data.]

7. REPORTS WORKING GROUP MISSION REVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katherine reviewed the working group's mission:

  Reports Working Group Mission:
  1. Document optimal Reports functionality within a future Evergreen release
     and develop a list of requirements.
  2. Become the Reports testing group, through which all new Reports development
     would be filtered.
  3. Compile a list of reports needed for an Executive Reports Interface.
  4. Determine and create templates needed for all PINES libraries.

All members agreed the mission is still accurate and relevant.

8. ACTION ITEMS AND NEXT STEPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - Technical subcommittee meeting: June 30, 2009 (Katherine to send agenda)
  - Complete draft of requirements document: by September 1, 2009
  - Katherine to circulate consolidated requirements list
  - George and Dana to draft technical architecture section
  - All members to continue gathering detailed report requirements

Meeting adjourned at 12:00 PM.

Minutes prepared by: Katherine Gregory, PINES Services Specialist
Minutes distributed: July 22, 2009"
 }

candidates.name: Consortium-Scale Operations
candidates.description: The management processes must support a library consortium with 286 locations, 17 million annual circulations, and purchasing and processing of more than 900,000 items per year.

candidates.name: Background Report Processing
candidates.description: The system must process searches and reports in the background or through a queue so that report generation during open or peak hours does not slow down circulation-client operations or other system functions.

candidates.name: Linux Solaris Server Support
candidates.description: The management processes must operate on either a Linux or Solaris server.

candidates.name: Browser Client Access
candidates.description: The management processes must be accessible through a web browser or a Windows-compatible client. Browser-based access must support Microsoft Internet Explorer version 6.0 or later and Mozilla Firefox version 2.0 or later.

candidates.name: Assistive Technology Access
candidates.description: The management processes must be accessible using screen-reading, screen-magnification, and other accessibility software, including JAWS, NVDA, and ZoomText, and must satisfy Section 508 requirements.
candidates.source_priority_note: D18 describes this as a legal requirement and says Section 508 compliance is mandatory.

candidates.name: Inventory Capacity Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide inventory and capacity reports for library staff who use them to monitor collections and operational capacity.

candidates.name: Financial Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide financial reports for library directors and other users who need director-level financial information.

candidates.name: Cross-Branch Comparisons
candidates.description: The system must provide reports that compare relevant library data across branches so library management can evaluate branches against one another.

candidates.name: Report Queue Visibility
candidates.description: The system must allow users to view the status and contents of the report-processing queue so they can monitor reports awaiting or undergoing processing.

candidates.name: Executive Report Definitions
candidates.description: The system must provide predefined reports for boards and executive users, supporting recurring executive-level reporting needs.

candidates.name: Data Quality Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide data quality reports that help library staff identify and assess problems in the system's data.

candidates.name: Card Swipe Login
candidates.description: The system must support staff login using a card swipe so staff can authenticate without relying solely on manually entered credentials.

candidates.name: In-Transit Item Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide reports on items in transit so library staff can coordinate delivery between locations.
candidates.source_priority_note: D18 describes in-transit item reports as critical for delivery coordination.

candidates.name: Missing Damaged Item Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide reports of missing and damaged items, with results available per branch so branch staff can manage local item problems.

candidates.name: Weeding Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide weeding reports that help library staff identify materials for collection-weeding activities.

candidates.name: Shelf Space Utilization
candidates.description: The system must provide reports showing shelf-space utilization so library staff can assess and plan physical collection capacity.

candidates.name: Demographic Analysis Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide demographic analysis for library staff planning programs and services.

candidates.name: Relational Database Backend
candidates.description: The management processes must use a fully relational database backend and operate correctly with the relational data structure used by the reporting layer.

candidates.name: Standards-Compliant HTML
candidates.description: The system must produce valid, standards-compliant HTML for report displays, the help system, and web-based user-interface components.

candidates.name: Configuration Migration Environments
candidates.description: The product must provide separate development and training environments and support migrating configurations, including report templates, between those environments and production through export and import.

candidates.name: Role-Based Access Control
candidates.description: The system must control user rights and privileges through security groups or roles, with access control applicable to individuals, workgroups, and arbitrary staff groups.

candidates.name: OPAC Functionality Preservation
candidates.description: Changes and functionality in the management processes must not constrain or adversely affect the functionality or features of the Online Public Access Catalog.

candidates.name: Record Data Specifications
candidates.description: The product must provide complete data specifications for authority, bibliographic, order, item, hold/request, and other records maintained or accessed by the management processes, enabling staff to understand the data structures used for queries.

candidates.name: Process Overview Documentation
candidates.description: The product must provide thorough high-level documentation of major processes, including bibliographic-record import and export, validation of bibliographic records against internal and external authority sources, and standard reports.

candidates.name: Online Cross-Linked Help
candidates.description: The system must provide online HTML help that is hierarchical and cross-linked, describes and illustrates all system functions, and is available without requiring staff to leave the system.

candidates.name: Actionable Error Feedback
candidates.description: The system must provide thorough high-level error reporting and feedback and must provide low-level, query-specific feedback through the front-end interface to Local and Global System Administrators when report or query operations fail.

candidates.name: Vendor Data Interfaces
candidates.description: The management processes must interface with external vendor websites through published APIs and/or automated transfers of standard-format data files, including formats such as USMARC21 and EDIFACT.

candidates.name: Acquisitions Cataloging Integration
candidates.description: The management processes must use the data structures and functionality of the enterprise library automation system's Acquisitions and Cataloging modules when reporting on acquisitions and cataloging data.

candidates.name: OPAC Data Querying
candidates.description: The management processes must interact with the Online Public Access Catalog and query patron-related data created there, including holds and circulation data.

You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.

================================================================================

Survey Period: April 1 - April 20, 2009
Survey Method: Online questionnaire distributed via PINES Connect portal
Respondents: 142 library staff members from 58 PINES member libraries
Response Rate: 34% (expected ~30%)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SURVEY QUESTIONS AND KEY FINDINGS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

QUESTION 1: "How frequently do you use reports from the current Evergreen
            system?"
  - Daily: 42%
  - Weekly: 28%
  - Monthly: 18%
  - Rarely: 9%
  - Never: 3%

QUESTION 2: "Which types of reports do you use most often? (Select all that
            apply)"
  - Circulation reports (checkouts, check-ins, renewals): 78%
  - Item reports (inventory, weeding, missing): 65%
  - Patron reports (demographics, inactive accounts): 52%
  - Financial reports (fines, payments): 34%
  - Hold reports (placed, filled, stale): 41%
  - Custom/on-demand reports: 29%

QUESTION 3: "What information do you need from transaction reports?"
Open-ended responses were categorized:

  Transactions can be grouped by hour, terminal, branch, and system.
  Transactions include check-ins, check-outs, fines collected, patron
  registrations, etc.

  Specific mentions:
  - "I need to see check-in counts broken down by method - book drop vs
    terminal vs self-service"
  - "Check-out types should be counted separately - staff checkout, self
    checkout, staff renewal, self checkout renewal, online renewal, OPAC
    renewal"
  - "Holds reports should show how the hold was placed - at staff desk,
    at public computer, or remotely"
  - "Group transactions by hour to identify busy periods"
  - "Need total transactions report - per patron, per library, per system"

QUESTION 4: "What demographic analysis do you need?"
  - Transactions by geographical regions
  - Transactions by age ranges
  - Patron behavior analysis (how quickly books are returned, renewal rates)
  - Demographic statistics (must be anonymized - no personally identifiable info)
  - "I use demographic data to plan programming. Age ranges and zip codes
    are most useful."
  - "We need to predict patron behavior. How likely is a book to be renewed?
    What percent of check-outs are renewals?"

QUESTION 5: "Which features are most important in a reports interface?"
  - Ability to create report templates: 81%
  - Fine-grained permissions (who can create/run what): 76%
  - Ability to save and reuse queries: 73%
  - Report queue visibility (where my report is in the queue): 68%
  - Multiple output formats (Excel, CSV, HTML): 61%
  - Email delivery of reports: 45%
  - Ability to schedule recurring reports: 52%

QUESTION 6: "What technical issues do you currently face?"
Open-ended responses:
  - "Reports take too long to run during busy hours"
  - "I can't see if my report is still processing"
  - "The interface is confusing - I can't find the reports I need"
  - "I need to export to Excel but the data has too many duplicate rows"
  - "Can't filter by some fields that should be available"
  - "Need to pull specific MARC fields but they're spread across multiple rows"

QUESTION 7: "Do you use any custom or local reports?"
  - Yes: 38%
  - No: 62%
  Among those who use custom reports, the most common are:
  - Collection development reports
  - Program attendance tracking
  - Staff productivity reports (time spent per transaction)

QUESTION 8: "What administrative features do you need?"
  - Query for candidate materials: 44%
  - Save queries for repeated use: 58%
  - Manually select from query results: 39%
  - Change records to move items to new location: 31%
  - Revert items to original location: 18%
  - Count and track record deletions: 27%

QUESTION 9: "What additional reports or features would you like to see?"
Selected responses:
  - "Historical reporting - I want to see what the data looked like on a
    specific date in the past, even if the shelving location has changed"
  - "Pivot table output would be great"
  - "Real-time reporting for busy periods"
  - "Ability to cancel a scheduled or running report"
  - "All nulls and blank fields must be included in results"
  - "Need a snapshot bills report going back in time"
  - "Ability to indicate last circulation date on item reports"
  - "Checkin date/time should not include renewals"

================================================================================
SUMMARY OF KEY REQUIREMENTS IDENTIFIED
================================================================================

1. Transaction history maintained for X days (configurable), with monthly and
   annual aggregates retained indefinitely.

2. Transactions can be grouped by hour, terminal, branch, and system.

3. All types of check-in counted individually and cumulatively: book-drop,
   terminal, by user or self-service.

4. All types of check-out counted individually and cumulatively: staff checkout,
   self checkout, staff renewal, self checkout renewal, online renewal, OPAC
   renewal.

5. Holds counted with method of placement: at staff desk, public computer,
   or remotely.

6. Transactions report can show holds placed, holds filled, and check-outs per
   patron, per library, per group of libraries, per system, per county.

7. Demographic statistics include transactions by geographical regions and age
   ranges. Data must be anonymized.

8. System produces statistics to understand/predict patron behavior and use
   of materials.

9. Report templates can be created by administrators and run as-is or modified.

10. Fine-grained permissions limit who can create and clone reports.

11. Shared folders to allow/disallow staff from running specific reports.

12. Ability to see where your report is in the queue.

Survey conducted by: Katherine Gregory, PINES Services Specialist
Results compiled: April 25, 2009
Report distributed to: PINES Reports Working Group"
 }
}

candidates.name: Retain Transaction History
candidates.description: The system must retain detailed transaction history for a configurable number of days and preserve monthly and annual aggregate data indefinitely.

candidates.name: Group Transactions By Dimensions
candidates.description: The system must group transaction reports by hour, terminal, branch, and system so staff can analyze activity and identify busy periods.

candidates.name: Count Check-In Methods
candidates.description: The system must count check-ins both individually and cumulatively by method, including book drop, terminal, staff/user processing, and self-service.

candidates.name: Count Checkout Types
candidates.description: The system must count check-outs both individually and cumulatively by type, including staff checkout, self checkout, staff renewal, self checkout renewal, online renewal, and OPAC renewal.

candidates.name: Classify Hold Placement
candidates.description: The system must report holds according to their placement method, including staff desk, public computer, and remote placement.

candidates.name: Aggregate Transaction Totals
candidates.description: The system must report holds placed, holds filled, and check-outs per patron, per library, per group of libraries, per system, and per county.

candidates.name: Provide Demographic Statistics
candidates.description: The system must provide transaction statistics by geographical region, age range, and useful demographic attributes such as ZIP code, while anonymizing the data so that personally identifiable information is not disclosed.

candidates.name: Analyze Patron Behavior
candidates.description: The system must produce statistics that help staff understand and predict patron behavior and material use, including return speed, renewal rates, the percentage of check-outs that are renewals, and the likelihood that a book will be renewed.

candidates.name: Create Report Templates
candidates.description: Administrators must be able to create report templates that can be run as-is or modified before execution.

candidates.name: Control Report Permissions
candidates.description: The system must provide fine-grained permissions that limit who can create, clone, and run particular reports.

candidates.name: Manage Shared Report Folders
candidates.description: The system must provide shared folders that can allow or prevent staff from running specific reports.

candidates.name: Show Report Queue Position
candidates.description: The system must show a user where the user's report is in the processing queue and whether it is still processing.

candidates.name: Save Reusable Queries
candidates.description: The system must allow staff to save queries and reuse them for repeated reporting activities.

candidates.name: Export Multiple Formats
candidates.description: The system must allow reports to be exported in Excel, CSV, and HTML formats, with Excel exports avoiding unnecessary duplicate rows.

candidates.name: Deliver Reports By Email
candidates.description: The system must support delivering completed reports by email.

candidates.name: Schedule Recurring Reports
candidates.description: The system must allow users to schedule reports to run on a recurring basis.

candidates.name: Query Candidate Materials
candidates.description: The system must allow staff to query for materials that are candidates for administrative actions.

candidates.name: Select Query Results Manually
candidates.description: The system must allow staff to manually select individual records from query results for subsequent administrative actions.

candidates.name: Move Items By Location
candidates.description: The system must allow authorized staff to change item records so that items are moved to a new location.

candidates.name: Revert Item Locations
candidates.description: The system must allow authorized staff to revert items to their original locations.

candidates.name: Track Record Deletions
candidates.description: The system must count and track record deletions.

candidates.name: Report Historical Data
candidates.description: The system must provide historical reporting that shows what data looked like on a specified past date, including historical shelving locations even when those locations have since changed.

candidates.name: Provide Snapshot Bills Reports
candidates.description: The system must provide a snapshot bills report that can retrieve bills information from past points in time.

candidates.name: Generate Pivot Outputs
candidates.description: The system must provide pivot-table output for reports.

candidates.name: Support Real-Time Reporting
candidates.description: The system must provide real-time reporting for activity during busy periods.

candidates.name: Cancel Running Reports
candidates.description: The system must allow users to cancel scheduled reports and reports that are currently running.

candidates.name: Include Empty Report Fields
candidates.description: The system must include null and blank fields in report results rather than excluding those records or values.

candidates.name: Expose Specific MARC Fields
candidates.description: The system must allow reports to retrieve specific MARC fields even when the fields are stored across multiple rows.

candidates.name: Show Last Circulation Date
candidates.description: The system must include the last circulation date as a field in item reports.

candidates.name: Exclude Renewals From Check-In Dates
candidates.description: The system must ensure that check-in date and time reporting does not include renewal transactions.

messages.content:
You are a requirements analyst. The user message is JSON with one input document (id, path, full text): an e-mail thread, interview, meeting minutes, survey, draft specification or reference material about a software system.

Extract every software requirement the document states or clearly implies: functional requirements, feature requests, constraints (technical, legal, organisational) and quality requirements (performance, security, usability, reliability, ...), one candidate per distinct requirement, sized by the definition at the end.

- Options, fields, filters, sort orders, display rules, thresholds and similar details of one capability belong inside that capability's description, never in a separate requirement. Several distinct capabilities are never one requirement, even when they come from the same document, thread or stakeholder; sharing a topic is not a reason to merge.
- Only explicit asks or clearly implied needs count. An open question, a complaint without a request, an aside, or a remark about what people do is not a requirement, and you add no capability the source does not mention (for example no extra operators or options for a query tool). Skip small talk and project process (meeting schedules, who should be interviewed, testing and QA process, assumptions about the team). Documentation and training that a source states as requirements of the software or product (for example user documentation items in a draft specification) are requirements and are kept.
- Never write a pointer requirement: a requirement states the capability itself, never "the reports listed in the specification/appendix", "see section X" or "the examples identified in ...". When a source contains a catalogue or list of items (for example an appendix of report types), each item becomes its own requirement or is explicitly folded into a named requirement whose description covers it.
- Work on this document only: do not judge whether a request is good, feasible or consistent. A request that is later rejected or contradicted inside the document is still a candidate; describe the disagreement in its description.
- Each requirement has a short descriptive name (3 to 8 words) and a one-paragraph description that keeps the concrete facts (numbers, fields, roles). The description says what the system must do or satisfy, who needs it and why, using the document's own facts.
- The description states only what the system must do or be: no provenance (which document, who said it) and no priority prose. Source priority signals go in source_priority_note instead: when a source marks the item with an explicit priority marker (for example [*] or "High") or calls it critical, mandatory, legally required or non-negotiable, write a short note naming the document id (for example "D10 marks this High; D06 calls it critical"); otherwise null. A note describes only its own item: never attach a signal a source gives for a different capability.

Definition of a requirement: A requirement describes one capability, rule or quality the system must provide, at the level a tester would write one acceptance test for. It names what, for whom, and under what condition, and it is independent of how it is implemented. Two statements are the same requirement if a tester would write one test for both. A statement is too broad if its acceptance test would have to be several unrelated tests. A statement is too narrow if it only makes sense as a detail of another requirement, such as one filter option of a report.

Example of a statement that is too broad: "Staff can manage item transfers between branches, including selecting candidate items by circulation history and keeping an audit history of every completed transfer." This is exactly two requirements: (1) select transfer candidates by circulation history, (2) record an audit history of completed transfers.
Example of statements that are too narrow: "The inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch" and "The inactive patron report can be filtered by patron profile". These are one requirement: the inactive patron report can be filtered by home branch and patron profile.
